passages.happening:
Some elders of Israel come and sit before Ezekiel. God tells him, ‘these men have set up idols in their hearts and put wicked stumbling blocks before their faces. Should I consult with them in any way?’ (verse 3). When anyone with idols in his heart comes to a prophet, God himself will answer him, to take hold of the hearts of a people estranged by their idols (verses 4-5).

‘Repent and turn away from your idols’ (verse 6). Anyone who keeps his idols and still comes to inquire will find God's face set against him (verses 7-8). If a prophet is enticed to give such a person a word, God says he has enticed that prophet, and both will bear their punishment (verses 9-10), ‘in order that the house of Israel may no longer stray from Me’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Consulting a prophet was a normal part of ancient religion. Kings and ordinary people went to prophets or diviners before important decisions. Across the ancient world it was assumed that one could approach several gods and several sources of guidance. These elders had not given up the LORD, but they had set up idols in their hearts and wanted a word from his prophet as well.

An idol in the heart is the inward side of idolatry: a loyalty that has moved before any image is made. God refuses to be one more counselor among many.
passages.later: In Ahab's day a spirit went out to be ‘a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets’ (1 Kings 22:22). The great commandment calls for love of God with all the heart (Deuteronomy 6:5).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that God entices a prophet to speak falsely and then punishes him (verse 9)?

This verse troubles many readers, and several answers have been given. One reads it in the light of 1 Kings 22, where God allows a lying spirit to deceive prophets who already wanted to tell the king what he wished to hear: God gives people over to the deception they have chosen, which itself becomes judgment. A second notes that Hebrew often speaks of God as the cause of everything that happens, including what he permits, without the distinctions later theology makes. A third stresses the setting: a prophet who gives a comforting word to someone with idols in his heart is already compromised, and God's judgment exposes him.

All three agree that the verse does not make God a deceiver of the innocent. The text ties the prophet's fate to the inquirer's and says the purpose is that Israel would no longer stray (verse 11).
passages.asks: The elders wanted God's word while keeping their idols. Ask whether you come to God for guidance you have already decided to ignore. And ask what idol you would need to put down first.

passages.happening:
If a land sins against God and he sends famine, wild beasts, the sword or plague, then even if Noah, Daniel and Job were in it, ‘their righteousness could deliver only themselves’ (verse 14). They could not save even their own sons or daughters (verses 16-20).

How much worse when God sends all four judgments against Jerusalem (verse 21). Yet some survivors will come out, sons and daughters, and when the exiles see their ways they will be consoled, and know that God did nothing ‘without cause’ (verses 22-23).
passages.hearers:
The idea that a few righteous people could protect a whole community ran deep. Abraham bargained over Sodom, and Moses prayed for Israel. Here God says that time is past for Jerusalem.

Noah and Job are well known; both lived outside Israel's covenant history. Who Daniel is is debated. The Hebrew spells the name Dan'el, slightly differently from the prophet of the book of Daniel. Some identify him with that Daniel, taken to Babylon in 605 BC and known at court for wisdom and faithfulness. Others identify him with Danel, a righteous king and judge in a legend from the Canaanite city of Ugarit, from before 1200 BC, who would pair naturally with Noah and Job as ancient figures from outside Israel. Both views have serious defenders.

The four judgments are the covenant curses of Leviticus 26.
passages.later: ‘Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation’ (Genesis 6:9), and Job was ‘blameless and upright’ (Job 1:1). Jeremiah heard that even Moses and Samuel could not turn God's heart to this people (Jeremiah 15:1).
passages.asks: Even the most righteous could deliver only themselves. Ask what it means that no one can carry another's faith for them. And ask whom you are praying for while there is still time.
